passage:
"You sit next to Deepa," Manoj said, leaning on Rajni's desk. "Can you tell her the client presentation was a mess? She'll take it better from you."
"What was wrong with it?"
"Everything. And between us, the whole team thinks she's slow."
Rajni saved her file and turned her chair. "Manoj, I'm not going to pass that on."
"Come on, you two are friends."
"That's exactly why. If I carry it, she hears it twisted, and then she wonders what I think too. You saw the problems. You should tell her."
"She'll get defensive."
"Maybe. Tell her the three things you'd change, not the whole-team part. I'm happy to book the small meeting room for you two."
Manoj rubbed his face. "Fine. Book it for four."
"And Manoj? I'm not taking sides. If she asks me, I'll tell her to talk to you as well."

qa.q: What did Manoj want Rajni to tell Deepa?
qa.a: He wanted Rajni to tell Deepa the client presentation was a mess.

qa.q: Why did Rajni refuse to pass the message on?
qa.a: She worried that carrying it would twist it and make Deepa wonder what Rajni herself thought, damaging trust between them.

qa.q: Which suggestion from Rajni helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking Manoj to share his three changes directly and offering to book the small meeting room turned gossip into a real conversation between the two people involved.

qa.q: What might change for Deepa if she hears the feedback from Manoj himself?
qa.a: She gets specific points she can act on instead of a rumour about the whole team, and she can ask him questions directly.

grounding: A young woman at work refuses to carry a critical message about Deepa, suggests Manoj talk to Deepa directly, and declines to take sides.

passage:
For two months last year, my phone was a switchboard. My brother Harish would call after dinner: "Manjula, tell Sheela she's being unreasonable about the Pune job." An hour later his wife Sheela would message: "You know him best. Make him see sense."
I'm the middle child. Fixing things is my job, I thought. So I passed along softened versions, and somehow both of them grew angrier, and each suspected I secretly agreed with the other.
The night Sheela cried on the phone that Harish had "told me you called me selfish", I saw that I had become part of the fight.
The next day I called them separately and said the same words to each: "I'm stepping out of the middle. Please talk to each other directly, maybe with a counsellor's help. I'll still listen, but I won't take a side."
It felt cold at first. Then, slowly, they started talking.

qa.q: What did Harish want Manjula to tell Sheela?
qa.a: Harish wanted Manjula to tell Sheela she was being unreasonable about the Pune job.

qa.q: What did Manjula feel and realise the night Sheela cried?
qa.a: Manjula felt dismayed and guilty, realising the softened messages had made Manjula part of the fight rather than a peacemaker.

qa.q: What choice did Manjula make the next day, and why did it help?
qa.a: Manjula called both separately with the same words, stepping out of the middle and pointing them to talk directly, which stopped the twisting of messages.

qa.q: How might Sheela experience Manjula stepping back?
qa.a: At first it may have felt like losing an ally, but hearing that Harish got the same message showed Manjula was fair, and it pushed the couple to talk.

grounding: A person caught between a brother and his wife stops carrying their messages, urges them to talk directly, and declines to take a side.

passage:
Operations manager's note, Monday.
I overheard a conversation today that I want to note for Suraj's review.
Akash came to Suraj's desk upset. "Tell Priya she can't just change the rota without asking. She listens to you. And tell her everyone thinks she's bossy."
Suraj didn't take the message. He said, "I get that you're frustrated. But I'm not going to carry that to her. It'll sound worse coming from me, and I don't want to be in the middle. Why don't you talk to her directly? If you want, I'll sit in, but you'd do the talking."
Akash grumbled that Suraj was "no help." But half an hour later, I saw Akash and Priya in the small meeting room. The rota was sorted by lunch.
Suraj didn't take sides and didn't pass on the "bossy" comment. That kept things cleaner for everyone.

qa.q: What did Akash want Suraj to tell Priya about the rota?
qa.a: That she can't just change the rota without asking.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when Suraj refused?
qa.a: Akash felt frustrated and annoyed, grumbling that Suraj was no help.

qa.q: What did Suraj do that kept relationships cleaner?
qa.a: Suraj declined to carry the message or take sides, suggested Akash talk to Priya directly, and offered only to sit in.

qa.q: How might Priya have felt if Suraj had passed on the "bossy" comment?
qa.a: Priya would likely have felt hurt and defensive, and the conflict would have grown instead of being sorted by lunch.

grounding: A manager records an employee declining to carry a colleague's complaint and suggesting the two talk directly.

passage:
Wednesday night
At lunch today, Joseph leaned over and said, "You know Divya's been telling people you're slow with reports? Just thought you should know." Then: "Can you tell her the client hated her slides? You're friends. She'll take it better from you."
I felt my stomach drop, and then that old itch to go and confront Divya, or to pass on his message and watch her face.
I didn't. I said, "Joseph, if Divya has a problem with my reports, I'll ask her myself. And if the client hated the slides, it's better coming from you or from our manager, directly. I don't want to carry things between people."
He rolled his eyes. "Fine, Manjula. So principled."
Afterwards I went to Divya and asked plainly, "Is there anything about my reports you'd like to tell me?" She looked confused. "No? They're great."
So much trouble, avoided.

qa.q: What did Joseph say Divya had been telling people?
qa.a: That Manjula's slow with reports.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel when Joseph shared the gossip?
qa.a: Manjula felt shaken and tempted to confront Divya or pass on the message, before choosing not to.

qa.q: What did Manjula do instead of being a channel?
qa.a: Manjula refused to carry Joseph's message, said she'd ask Divya herself, and then asked Divya plainly.

qa.q: How did Divya react when Manjula asked her directly?
qa.a: Divya looked confused and said the reports were great, showing the gossip wasn't true.

grounding: A diary shows an adult refusing to carry gossip between colleagues and going back to the source directly.

passage: At the weekly haat in their village near Jorhat, Rajni caught Bhupen by the vegetable stalls. "You're close to Hemanta-da," she said, lowering her voice. "Tell him the self-help group knows he kept the best stall spot for his wife. Everyone's saying it. He'll listen to you." Bhupen set down his bag of brinjals. Hemanta-da and Rajni had been at odds since the Bihu committee. Carrying this, he could see, would make him a messenger in a quarrel he had never joined. "Baideo, if you think it's unfair, say it to him yourself," he said gently. "I can sit with you both after the group meeting on Sunday if that helps. But I won't carry a message either way, from you or from him." Rajni's mouth tightened. "So you're on his side." "I'm on nobody's side. That's the point." On Sunday, she came to the meeting early.

qa.q: What did Rajni want Bhupen to tell Hemanta-da?
qa.a: That the self-help group knows he kept the best stall spot for his wife.

qa.q: What was Bhupen thinking as he set down the brinjals?
qa.a: Bhupen felt wary and uneasy, seeing that carrying the message would make him a messenger in a quarrel he had never joined.

qa.q: Why was offering to sit with them both a wise move?
qa.a: It sent the complaint back to its source while still offering support, and refusing messages from either side kept Bhupen out of the fight.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt when Bhupen refused?
qa.a: Rajni felt rebuffed and suspicious at first, accusing him of taking Hemanta-da's side, yet coming early on Sunday suggests she accepted talking directly.

grounding: Shows a person asked to carry a grievance who suggests the two talk directly and declines to take sides.
